highlights: Claude published a guide to building always-on agents, outlining five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox.

items.title: Claude Blog explains how to build always-on agents
items.summary: Always-on agents run indefinitely, deciding how and when to act across many sessions, and Claude's guide walks through their core primitives and how they fit together. The architecture rests on five primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox, giving developers a concrete blueprint for building stateful, proactive agents.

evidence.quote: Building always-on agents Always-on agents run indefinitely, deciding how and when to act across many sessions.
This guide walks through their core primitives and how they fit together.
Always-on agents are stateful and proactive, meaning they manage context across sessions and take actions without direct supervision.
Underneath, they run on the same core loop as other agents.
The difference is the surrounding architecture, which is built from primitives that control when the agents wake up, what carries over between runs, and how their work reaches the user.
The resurgence is largely due to recent model advancements, which have made always-on agents more practical to run.
First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in.
Second, intelligence is becoming cheaper, with long-horizon tasks benefiting the most.
For example, on one long-horizon coding benchmark , Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.
The core primitives The surrounding architecture of an always-on agent has five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox.
Timers Together with the event inbox, timers let always-on agents be proactive.
Memory Always-on agents work across many disjointed runs and rely on memory to maintain continuity.

items.title: IBM trains two small open models to ignore instructions hidden in documents
items.summary: IBM's Granite AI team released two preview models, granite-4.1-3b-llmon-preview and granite-4.1-8b-llmon-preview, trained with the LLMON labeling system to separate user instructions from document content. Both are open models under the Apache 2.0 license with downloadable weights, but IBM limits the previews to exploration and evaluation and advises against real-world use.

evidence.quote: On November 12, 2026, IBM’s Granite AI team released two preview models trained to ignore commands hidden in the documents they read.
Both rely on LLMON, an IBM labeling system that separates the user’s instructions from the material the model reads.
The two models, granite-4.1-3b-llmon-preview and granite-4.1-8b-llmon-preview, have 3.7 billion and 8.8 billion parameters.
Both are open models: anyone can download them from Hugging Face, a platform for sharing AI models.
Their license, Apache 2.0, allows commercial use.
IBM tested them on a public benchmark, a standard set of attacks.
Against the standard Granite 4.1 models, which lack this training, the attacks worked 96% to 100% of the time.
Against the previews, they worked at most 0.1% of the time.
Even so, IBM limits the previews to exploration and evaluation and advises against real-world use.
On OPI, the attack success rate drops from 100% for the standard 3B model to 0.1% for its preview, and from 96.3% to 0.02% for the 8B.
On ASB, it falls from 99.2% to 5.6% for the 3B and from 52.8% to 3.1% for the 8B.

items.title: Serving GLM-5.3 across two Nvidia DGX stations with vLLM
items.summary: Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting model weights and computation across both GPUs. The post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load.

evidence.quote: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM
Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs.
The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai ’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token.
At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU.
This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load.
Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs.
Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API.

items.title: APEX uses condition shifting for few-step streaming video generation
items.summary: APEX extends a streaming video generation method by replacing a separate fake-score network with condition shifting, removing the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. Evaluated on 180-second videos, it achieved higher video instruction fulfillment and visual aesthetics than S2-Avatar, with 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD under matched training settings.

evidence.quote: Papers arxiv:2611.14033 Copy markdown Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting Published on Nov 10 · Submitted by Deyuan Liu on Nov 11 #1 Paper of the day · Tsinghua University Upvote 88 +80 Authors: Deyuan Liu , Jungang Li , Kaiwen Zheng , Kai Jiang , Jintao Chen , Yaole Wang , Mi

ng Lin , Tao Lin , Jianfei Chen , Jun Zhu , Jintao Zhang Abstract APEX extends a streaming video generation method by replacing a separate fake-score network with condition shifting to estimate the generated distribution’s velocity field, improving instruction following and visual aesthetics while r
Distribution Matching Distillation ( DMD ) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network , which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator.
We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator.
The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters.
This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar 's frozen reference teacher , Self-Replay Forcing , and perceptual regularization .
We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner , with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison.
Compared with S2-Avatar , APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606).
Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD .

items.title: SparseRead cuts token use for agents reading external content
items.summary: SparseRead is a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model, using a Read Intent Protocol, Adaptive Reader Backends, and a Budgeted Read Gate with faithful full-view fallback. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, it reduced total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings.

evidence.quote: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
Title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents

Authors: Zedong Liu , Jiaan Wu , Xinyang Ma , Le Xu , Kai Wang , Yuanchao Hu , Dingwen Tao , Guangming Tan View a PDF of the paper titled Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents, by Zedong Liu and 7 other authors
Abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed.
We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model.

Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback.
Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings.
On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%.
Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

items.title: WorldFoundry unifies infrastructure for generative world models
items.summary: WorldFoundry is open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation of generative world models across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video , 3D and 4D , embodied action , and interactive world systems .

WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration , artifact management , and interactive visualization , while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols.
Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts.
The current catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with integration readiness and execution evidence recorded separately for each entry.

items.title: SplatAnything normalizes Gaussian spacing for feed-forward 3DGS
items.summary: SplatAnything introduces Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to give Gaussian prediction a more consistent spatial reference. The authors also establish a benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints, reporting state-of-the-art performance with strong gains under large variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

evidence.quote: Papers arxiv:2611.08264 Copy markdown SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes Published on Nov 5 · Submitted by hao yu on Nov 9 #3 Paper of the day · Zhejiang University Upvote 69 +61 Authors: Hao Yu , Zhenwei Wang , Yongzhen Hu , Yuning Gong , Jun

ta Wu , Xiaowei Zhou , Hujun Bao , Tengfei Wang , Chunchao Guo , Sida Peng Abstract SplatAnything applies Gaussian Spacing Normalization to canonicalize scene-level Gaussian spacing, yielding more consistent supervision and improved feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under varying scene scales and v

Generated by deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between nei
ghboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scale s and camera configurations .
This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets , leading to ambiguous supervision.

To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization ( GSNorm ), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction.
To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels , and challenging extrapolated viewpoints .

items.title: ARC routes AI agents across cloud and local models
items.summary: ARC, the Adaptive Routing Controller, reads an agent's conversation and produces signals for choosing a model and its reasoning effort, while keeping prediction separate from policy. The routing model predicts success and token usage so applications can apply their own prices, eligibility rules, and local threshold, and the paper's hybrid configuration retains 97.5% of Opus 5.5's quality at 92.9% lower cost.

evidence.quote: A decision model for routing AI agents across cloud and local models.
ARC—the Adaptive Routing Controller—reads an agent’s conversation and produces signals for choosing a model and its reasoning effort.
Applications combine those signals with their available models, prices, and policies to decide how to handle the next request.
ARC separates predictions from policy.
It predicts success and token usage; the application supplies model prices and decides how to balance quality, cost, and local execution.
Updating prices does not require retraining those predictors when the model and serving configuration stay fixed.
Compare eligible models by their predicted probability of completing a task.
Estimate uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output; apply the prices relevant to your deployment.
Compare the expected benefit and cost of supported reasoning settings within a model.
Identify the presence and types of sensitive information in the supplied input.
Classify requested operations and domains, allowing multiple labels.
Choose a policy
Sage and Swift are preset configurations of the same routing model.
Their utility policy chooses the eligible model with the highest predicted success value minus expected cost:
Utility = V × predicted success − expected cost
ARC Sage · V = 4.5
ARC Swift · V = 0.1
Uses an eligible local model when it clears a chosen predicted-success threshold; otherwise applies the configured fallback policy.
You can supply your own value of success, model prices, eligibility rules, and local threshold.
Across six benchmarks, the paper’s hybrid configuration retains 97.5% of Opus 5.5’s quality at 92.9% lower cost .
This uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and a multiple-DGX-Spark deployment setup, with a 0.85 prefer-local threshold.
